To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) performance measures are useful in the abuse liability assessment of drugs, (2) performance measures are not interchangeable with subjective measures, (3) performance measures can be used to quantify the overall profile of drug effects, (4) performance measures can provide useful information on the likelihood of drug abuse, (5) performance measures may provide information on the harmful effects of drugs, and (6) performance measures are sensitive to the pharmacological effects of drugs.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of psychoactive drugs on performance, and the use of performance tests to assess the abuse liability of these drugs.
the development of objective measures of drug abuse potential that are based on the behavioral and physiological effects produced by the drug.
the development of a battery of performance and physiological tests to assess the abuse liability of drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

performance and physiological measures are useful in the abuse liability assessment of a variety of drug classes and that they can provide important information regarding the overall profile and harmfulness of drug effects.
performance and physiological measures can be used to evaluate abuse liability and should be used in abuse liability testing.

abuse liability studies employing performance and/or physiological measures can provide valuable information for evaluating the abuse potential of drugs and that the utility of such measures is likely to increase as more studies are conducted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

performance measures can serve as a reference standard to compare the effects of different drugs on multiple behavioral dimensions, that physiological measures can provide information on the overall drug profile of effects and the potential for harmful effects, and that performance and physiological measures are not interchangeable and thus both are necessary to provide a complete abuse liability evaluation.

performance and physiological measures have been useful in evaluating the abuse liability of sedatives, amphetamine-like stimulants, cocaine, opioids, and cannabis, although there are limitations to their utility.

the use of performance and physiological measures can provide a more comprehensive assessment of abuse liability and thus may be useful for the evaluation of drugs that are being considered for development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of performance and physiological measures is essential for the comprehensive evaluation of abuse liability and that such measures should be used in the evaluation of any drug of abuse.
performance and physiological measures can provide valuable information in abuse liability evaluation and should be considered in the design and interpretation of abuse liability studies.
abuse liability evaluation can be enhanced by the inclusion of performance and physiological measures, which can be used to evaluate the overall profile and harmful effects of drug effects.
